relations: When the hands release the top vertex and slide to the sides, the sphere triangle remains intact on the surface.
If the hands rotate the held lattice in-plane, the apex shifts from pointing upward toward pointing left.
As the triangle rotates, the upper-right sphere chain stays fixed, confirming the motion is from the hands, not the camera.
caption: The video depicts a top-down view of a plain white surface where a pair of hands with gray sweater cuffs manipulates a flat triangular lattice assembled from shiny metallic spheres. A separate chain and cluster of the same spheres stays in place in the upper-right corner, indicating little or no camera movement. At the start of the excerpt both hands pinch the upper vertex of the apex-up triangle, holding it steady with only small finger adjustments. The hands then release the top corner and slide outward to grip the left and right sides, settling near the lower corners while the structure keeps its apex-up orientation. With the triangle held by these sides, the hands rotate the whole lattice in-plane, swinging the apex from pointing upward toward pointing left. The grips shift along the edges to match the new orientation as the rotation proceeds. Throughout, the upper-right sphere chain remains fixed, so the visible changes come from the hands turning the sphere triangle rather than from apparent camera motion.
